newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FORECAST - Riksbank to cut interest rates this week.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Riksbank to cut interest rates this week.

text.p: Sweden's Riksbank (central bank) is expected to cut all of its key interest rates this week, while both short and long market rates will continue to fall into the first half of 1997, analysts said on Monday.
"We believe the central bank will stick to its pattern (of rate cuts) for some time to come," Keld Holm, economist at Lehman Brothers told Reuters.
All 11 analysts polled by Reuters believe the Riksbank would trim its key repo rate for the 22nd time this year at Tuesday's weekly reverse repurchase operation.
Most of them believed the cut would bring the rate down to 4.85 percent from its current level of 4.95 percent.
This would mean the repo rate has fallen by over four percentage points to 8.91 percent at the start of 1996.

A cut of 10 basis points would bring the repo rate to within one 10-basis-point cut of the Riksbank's deposit rate, the floor rate of the central bank's three-tier interest rate corridor. It is now set at 4.75 percent.
The lending rate, the corridor's ceiling, is now 6.25 percent.
Consequently, most of the analysts polled expected to see a cut in the interest rate corridor at the Riksbank's next board meeting on Thursday.
These rates were last cut on August 15.
"The central bank board has said that inflation will probably be lower than seen in the (September) inflation report," said Merrill Lynch analyst Richard Woodworth.
"If they are going to be able to continue cutting the repo rate, it's also high time for a reduction in the interest corridor."
Nine of the 11 believed the corridor would be lowered by 50 basis points, and one expected the central bank to cut it by as much as 75 basis points.
Most analysts expect the repo rate to bottom out at between 4.00 percent and 4.60 percent in early 1997.
This would bring short market rates with it. The rate on the six-month treasury bill is seen falling by around 20 basis points from Monday's level of 4.55 percent.
This, too, is expected to bottom out in the coming three months, after which the rate is seen increasing to 4.67 percent after twelve months.
Longer rates are also expected to fall, with the nine-year bond yield falling to 7.06 percent within the coming three months and then continuing down to 6.85 percent.
Analysts said the nine-year yield would bottom out at that level and return to 7.42 percent in a year's time.
